why: The chart labels a song count for each of the ten names. The ranks and nine of the ten counts reproduce from data/allNames.csv, but Heaven is credited with 61 songs in the chart and has 62 distinct songs (artist + song) in the file; the other counts match (Jesus 142, John 82, Mary 73, Joe 73, Michael 69, Jay 65, Bobby 62, Mike 62, Jack 58). The reproducible ranking is recorded as a fact, but the full per-item count finding is not reproduced exactly.

source: Only a handful of the most popular names over time have been typically women’s names.
why: The data has no gender field for names, so the proportion of typically women's names among the decade leaders cannot be computed from data/allNames.csv.

source: The top 5 name-dropping artists are all hip hop or rap musicians
why: The data has no genre field, so the claim that the five leading artists all belong to hip hop or rap cannot be checked from data/allNames.csv.

source: Names that start with A are much more common in society than in song lyrics
why: This compares song-name shares with the share of names used in US society. The society baseline comes from the SSA/onlyNames.csv name-frequency data, which is not in this folder; data/allNames.csv alone cannot produce the comparison.

source: Apart from Jesus, these names have a long history of popularity in the US. While many of these names hit their peak popularity in the 1950s
why: This is a claim about the year-by-year popularity of names in the US from Social Security Administration data, which is not in this folder; data/allNames.csv contains only names found in song lyrics.

source: with Michael and John still ranking as the 8th and 26th and most common boy’s names in the US in 2016, respectively.
why: The US 2016 boy's-name rankings come from the Social Security Administration's baby-name data, not from data/allNames.csv.
